text: Hi, I'm Ramona J. Smith, Toastmasters  International 2018 World Champion of
Public Speaking. I know first hand how gestures  and body language. I know first-hand how gestures
and body language can help to captivate  an audience because I'm one of millions
of people who Toastmasters has helped gain the  confidence to communicate in all circumstances.
As a speaker, you know that the messages  your words convey can be helped or hurt by
the messages your body sends. To be truly  successful in communication, you must be
in command of your hand gestures, posture,  facial expressions, and overall body language.
Today, I'm going to share some great tips  that will help you master your movements.
Calm nerves with practice.
Have you ever been in front of an audience  and had trouble letting go of a lectern?
Nervous mannerisms can mean trouble for  speakers. For example, shifting your weight,
adjusting your glasses, wringing your hands.  These are all things you might do that lessen
the impact of your presentations and, oh!  Tugging at your clothes; that's a problem, too.
You'd be surprised how nervous tics and  inconsistent body language can distract
an audience. Gestures that don t coordinate  well with a speaker's message can drain the
speaker's energy and shift the audience's  focus away from the intended message.
So, what should a speaker do? The  answer is planning and practice.
The more you rehearse your speech, the better idea  you'll have for gestures that emphasize a point.
For example, if you want to explain to a group  that your new home is very far from your family,
you could extend one arm out from your  body while placing your other hand on your
heart to demonstrate the distance. This  descriptive gesture conveys the message
of distance while suggesting the idea  that your home is far from your heart.
Knowing that you're going to perform this  gesture at a targeted moment in your speech
will guide you as you prepare. When you  perform planned gestures in a speech,
you'll be able to channel nervous energy into  constructive movements that support your ideas.
Types of gestures What kinds of
gestures should you imagine when planning a  speech? Think of them in four major groups.
First, descriptive gestures , like the one  I just used, help make your words clearer.
They can help describe things like the size,  shape, and location of objects you're discussing.
Second, emblematic gestures  are culturally specific,
though some are universal  such as nodding and shrugging.
Emblematic movements underscore strong  emotion such as earnestness and conviction.
In many cultures placing your hand on your heart  communicates a powerful belief in your message.
Third, representational gestures include movements  that give information about what you re doing.
You might use your hands to demonstrate  chopping, throwing, or picking something up.
And fourth, pantomime gestures are a good way  to ask your audience to participate or respond.
If you want them to raise their hands, for  example, you may raise your hand to show them.
Well, that's a lot of gestures, isn't  it? And that's good. For all the choices,
you can select those gestures that  naturally fit what you want to say.
Start by thinking about the ways you normally  move and try to rehearse those movements that come
naturally for you. If you feel you have to force  something that doesn't come from your instinctive
whole-body movements, think of another gesture or  movement that feels more natural to your style.
Movements such as this are probably not expressive
enough to be in your speech. Instead, think of  gestures that support the ideas in your talk.
Try to focus your thoughts on the words  you share from one point to the next.
Consider movements that are a natural response  to your thoughts, feelings, and words.
A word of caution when planning your gestures.  Some gestures that are perfectly appropriate
in one culture are offensive in another. It's  important to know your audience and plan your
gestures well.
Coordination
Coordinating gestures, eye contact, and  movement can be a challenge for any speaker.
When you present to an in-person audience, you  will need to practice making eye contact while
walking across a stage. It is another set of  skills entirely to coordinate gestures and
make eye contact while meeting fully online  or with virtual attendees and an in-person
audience during a hybrid meeting. Those skills  take time to develop in front of your webcam.
No matter how you meet in-person, fully online,  or hybrid take the time to practice with your
equipment or arrive early and walk around. With your planned and rehearsed gestures,
you'll be able to let go of the lectern in no  time, and give your speech the impact it deserves.
